extracted.intended_audience: academics, students, and documentary/photojournalism practitioners interested in visual narrative, ethics, and photographic history
extracted.subtask_description: Analysing and critiquing how photographic images function as narratives—their ethics, techniques, social impact and role in collective memory—with emphasis on documentary/photojournalism practice. The guidance is aimed at understanding what makes photographs effective, persuasive, or problematic as visual stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photography as narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Photography tells visual stories about the world and 'is narrating the world' by representing situations, events, persons, moods and atmospheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs function as a form of narration (Jacobson 1998). Evaluate whether an image conveys a coherent narrative about its subject and whether it situates that subject in a comprehensible situation, event or mood. Examples: work by Sebastiao Salgado, James Nachtwey, Don McCullin as recognised visual storytellers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photograph's ability to convey narrative independently of text
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs can convey narrative without accompanying text and people routinely use images to build stories and store memories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the image communicates meaning or story without explanatory captions, and whether it has been 'transformed' to touch emotions rather than merely showing (Batchen 2005). Consider how viewers construct narratives from visual cues alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arresting time / restorative memory function
rubrics_metrics.description: A photograph's power to 'arrest time' and 'restore the past', acting as a trail or 'ghost trail' of memories that brings past moments back to life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how effectively an image functions as a mnemonic or 'flashback'—its capacity to implant or trigger long-term memory (Sontag, Newton). Examples: iconic images that become part of collective memory (Tiananmen man, Falling Man).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual inclusion and exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Any photographic narrative results from including some elements and excluding others; effective narrative requires knowing what is best included or excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how framing, cropping, sequencing and selection choices shape interpretation. Consider whether omissions mislead or whether contextual information is provided or necessary. Photographers should understand context to make responsible inclusion/exclusion decisions (Campbell 2010).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proficiency in research and contextual knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentary visual storytellers need to be highly proficient researchers who understand the historical, cultural, social and technical contexts of their subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the depth of background research and contextualization evident in the images or accompanying material. Lack of context is an anti-pattern; rigorous inquiry underpins credible documentary work (Campbell 2010; Newton 2001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs as evidence and record
rubrics_metrics.description: Photography can serve as an exposé and a document of record—bearing witness to events, institutions and abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether images function as credible evidence (e.g., child labour, war atrocities). Check for authenticity, corroboration, and how the photo has been used to prompt public or institutional response (e.g., Salgado's Serra Pelada, McCullin, Brady).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and civic responsibility / bearing witness
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers bear moral responsibilities when showing suffering or injustice; bearing witness cultivates historical sense and can have moral dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate photographer intent, respect for subjects, and whether images encourage thoughtful engagement rather than voyeuristic consumption. Examples: photographers aiming to 'name the nameless' and give voice to the voiceless (Nachtwey, Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional impact and capacity to prompt action
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful images evoke strong emotions and can mobilise audiences or resources, though images alone seldom change the world without other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess emotional potency and whether the image is likely to inspire engagement or practical responses (e.g., Stoddart's famine photos prompting hotline calls). Avoid overclaiming that a single image will cause systemic change; consider the wider context of impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding exploitative 'tourism of poverty'
rubrics_metrics.description: Images of suffering should not be exploitative; ethical documentary work penetrates human spirit rather than violating or commodifying suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for dignity in portrayal, consent where possible, avoidance of sensationalism, and evidence that the work serves a cause rather than 'poverty tourism' (Galeano on Salgado; Linfield). Staged or intrusive images (Riis examples) can be ethically problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity vs staging (means vs ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers sometimes stage scenes to suit storytelling purposes; the ethical and narrative legitimacy of staging must be scrutinised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate practices like staging or invasions of privacy (Riis) as potential anti-patterns. Determine whether staging undermines credibility or whether it was justified and disclosed; transparency is key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of codes, conventions, and cultural framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs are invested with structures of codes and conventions that mediate how viewers interpret images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the photographer understands and ethically manipulates visual codes (composition, lighting, symbols) and whether cultural framings might distort or clarify meaning (Clarke 1997). Consider cross-cultural misreading risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived objectivity and constructed meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Photography's perceived objectivity can recommend it to an empirical age, but images also operate at the level of connotation and reflect the photographer's investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine claims of objectivity and consider how sequencing, captioning, and selection construct meaning (Sekula 1982). Treat photographic 'truth' as constructed and open to interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographer as ethnographer / immersive practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers often act like ethnographers—immersing themselves in cultures to record and reflect meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the photographer demonstrates immersion, sustained engagement, and cultural sensitivity (Newton 2001). Shallow, opportunistic imaging is a weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to audience information needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The best documentary photographs relate to the desires of their audience for information and act as a mirror to past events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how well images communicate information the audience needs and whether they enhance public understanding (Price 2004). Images primarily serving aesthetic ends may fail documentary purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics of showing graphic/deceased subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: There are powerful prohibitions and sensitivities around showing naked faces of the dead or graphic depictions; such choices carry ethical weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate necessity, public interest, respect for victims and families, and potential harm. Historical practice shows both censorship and powerful disclosure (Brady, Sontag on interdiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing to emphasise the significant (removing the superfluous)
rubrics_metrics.description: A camera can 'remove the superfluous and focus the attention' so that only significant and characteristic aspects are seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess compositional choices that distill the scene to its characteristic elements (Rothstein). Over-cluttered or unfocused images dilute narrative efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs as part of collective memory and conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Images enter collective consciousness and conscience, becoming constituent parts of what a society chooses to think about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether an image is likely to have lasting cultural resonance and whether it responsibly shapes collective memory (Sontag, Goldberg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Photography's dual role: information and moral vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentary photography delivers both factual information and a moral/radical vocabulary that can speak to public conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the balance between factual reporting and moral argument; strong documentary work often combines clear information with a moral stance (Nachtwey, Salgado).

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs as catalysts for discussion rather than standalone solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs can catalyse discussion and awareness but typically operate alongside other factors to produce change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate images as part of broader communicative strategies—campaigns, reporting, policy advocacy—rather than expecting solitary impact (Campbell 2010).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual storytelling's relation to other texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentary photographs have a special relationship to other texts and are often used to narrate events or illustrate written news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how images interact with captions, articles, reports and whether the combination provides fuller, responsible narrative (Price 2004). Images divorced from context risk misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics of publication and editorial gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions by editors and agencies about publishing graphic or contentious images reflect ethical judgments and affect public exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider editorial reluctance or decisions (e.g., agencies initially not publishing Jarecke's Gulf War photo) as part of the ethical evaluation. Transparency about editorial choices and rationale is valuable.
